summary:
We have created the Lunar Landing Site Navigator—an interactive tool for comparing landing sites and dates at five polar locations on the Moon. It addresses this challenge by combining data on the horizon’s topography with the positions of the Sun and Earth to help assess the availability of solar energy and direct communication with Earth.



Users can explore the surface on a 3D globe, track conditions on a timeline, compare scenarios, and search for multi-year landing windows while taking mission requirements into account. The tool also shows how a launch delay affects available windows.



The project is important because Earth’s illumination and visibility depend on the time of day and local terrain, and thus can affect a mission’s power supply and communications. By presenting these relationships in an accessible, comparable format, Navigator supports more informed decision-making regarding future landings.
details:
Detailed Project Description

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a web application that helps users quickly assess and compare landing conditions at five polar locations on the Moon. It was developed in response to a NASA Space Apps challenge to clearly visualize the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local horizon—information that is essential for planning power supply and direct communication with Earth.

What does it do and how does it work?

The Navigator combines terrain and horizon data with calculations of the positions of celestial bodies. It offers five complementary views:
Sky displays a 360° panoramic view of the horizon and the paths of the Sun and Earth.

Timeline lets you track changes in altitude and visibility over time.

Compare allows you to compare up to four landing scenarios.

Windows helps you search for multi-year landing windows between 2027 and 2035, apply mission requirements, and check the impact of launch delays.

Map displays an interactive 3D globe, facilitates exploration of the poles, and visualizes zones with varying visibility conditions.

The application takes into account, among other things, the terrain profile on the horizon, sunlight availability, Earth visibility, eclipses, and horizon measurement uncertainty. In the map view, you can compare zones and candidates based on the results of a mission profile adjusted by weights. The data includes LOLA horizon profiles and calendars for five locations; after downloading NAIF kernels, calculations use SPICE, and without them, the app switches to an approximate model.

Technology and Creativity

The backend is written in Python, using FastAPI, NumPy, and SPICEypy. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, and Three.js, and the project is built and run using Vite. A NASA LROC texture is used to visualize the globe. The project is software-based—the repository does not indicate the use of any special hardware.

Creativity involves combining a 3D map, a view of the local horizon, a timeline, and a comparison tool into a single navigation system, as well as presenting potential zones as condition maps and rankings. This allows the same data to be viewed both spatially and in the context of time and the requirements of a specific mission.
